Day 1
From Hotel: 11 min → Forte de Copacabana
1. Forte de Copacabana
Built at the southern tip of Copacabana Beach with 360-degree views of the Atlantic and Guanabara Bay. Its museum documents the Revolta dos 18 do Forte, when eighteen officers marched against government troops on this beach in one of Brazil's defining modern political moments.

20 min · 5 min → Praia de Ipanema
2. Praia de Ipanema
The arc of Ipanema stretches from the Arpoador rock west toward Leblon, backed by the twin peaks of Dois Irmãos. Each section of the beach has its own character — Post 9 draws families, Post 8 LGBTQ+ crowds, and the far end athletic groups. Mornings are the locals' hour before vendors and visitors arrive.

25 min → Sugarloaf Mountain
3. Sugarloaf Mountain
Two cable cars — first to Morro da Urca, then to the 396-metre granite summit — deliver the view that makes Rio's layout comprehensible: the bay behind Niterói, the arc of Copacabana, Christ in the green hinterland, and the Atlantic beyond. Cable cars have run here since the early 20th century.

1. Confeitaria Colombo
The grandest café interior in the Americas — gilded mirrors from Belgium, stained-glass skylights, ornate jacaranda wood counters, and a salon where the city's writers, politicians, and presidents met for over a century.

11 min · 5 min → Theatro Municipal
2. Theatro Municipal
Rio's 1909 Beaux-Arts opera house, modelled on the Paris Opéra Garnier, was built on 1,180 wooden piles driven into the groundwater. The gilded interior holds the main auditorium, a Assyrian Room, and a Salão Nobre decorated with works by Henrique Bernardelli. Guided tours run weekdays and Saturday afternoons.

16 min · 6 min → Royal Portuguese Cabinet of Reading
3. Royal Portuguese Cabinet of Reading
Founded in 1837 by Portuguese immigrants, this Neo-Manueline library holds the largest collection of Portuguese-language works outside Portugal. The interior — a four-storey iron gallery topped by a stained-glass skylight — was ranked by Time among the world's four most beautiful libraries.

24 min · 6 min → National Historical Museum
4. National Historical Museum
Over 287,000 artifacts trace Brazilian history from 1603 to the present, housed in a fort complex whose first walls date to 1567. Highlights include the largest numismatic collection in Latin America, Dom Pedro I's coronation regalia, and the courtyard cannons of the original São Tiago fort.

5. Museu do Amanhã
Santiago Calatrava's science museum extends over Guanabara Bay like a white skeletal wing, its solar fins tracking the sun. Five chapters — Cosmos, Earth, Anthropocene, Tomorrow, Us — use real-time data and interactives to put the future of civilisation in your hands.

Day 3
From Hotel: 15 min → Escadaria Selarón
1. Escadaria Selarón
Chilean artist Jorge Selarón tiled a crumbling Lapa staircase from the mid-1990s until his death, covering 215 steps with tile fragments collected from more than 60 countries. He called it his gift to the Brazilian people and never stopped adding to it.

2. Parque das Ruínas
A 19th-century mansion's skeletal iron frame and crumbling walls preserved on a Santa Teresa hilltop. The terrace overlooks Guanabara Bay, downtown skyscrapers, Maracanã, and Christ the Redeemer all at once — one of the finest panoramas in the city.

26 min · 9 min → Catete Palace
3. Catete Palace
Brazil's presidential palace from 1897 to 1960 is now the Museu da República. Fourteen presidents lived here; on 24 August 1954 Getúlio Vargas shot himself in the bedroom — the bullet hole, blood-stained pyjamas, and farewell letter remain on display. The garden with its pond and exotic trees is free to enter.

From Hotel: 11 min → Parque Lage
1. Parque Lage
An Italian Renaissance palace built by an industrialist for the soprano he loved, set against Atlantic Forest rising straight into Corcovado. From the arched central courtyard you can look up through the canopy and see Christ's back directly above. Now a public park housing Rio's School of Visual Arts.

2. Cristo Redentor
The Art Deco Christ stands with arms wide on the 709-metre summit of Corcovado — one of the most recognised monuments on earth. The view from the base, with all of Rio spread below in every direction, matches every expectation. Take the cog railway from Cosme Velho; it climbs through Atlantic Forest the whole way.

3. Cascatinha Taunay — Tijuca National Park
A 35-metre waterfall inside Tijuca National Park — the world's largest urban forest, 3,200 hectares entirely within Rio's city limits. The trail passes giant ferns, bromeliads, and marmosets. It is extraordinary to be this deep inside living Atlantic Forest ten minutes from Copacabana.

25 min → Tijuca National Park
4. Tijuca National Park
The world's largest urban rainforest covers 3,953 hectares above Rio. Over 40km of trails lead to waterfalls, granite peaks, and the Vista Chinesa — a pagoda viewpoint over the city's beaches and the Lagoa. Coffee farming stripped the hillside bare in the 18th century; the forest was replanted in the 19th.

Day 5
From Hotel: 15 min → Jardim Botânico
1. Jardim Botânico
A garden founded for spice acclimatisation that became one of the world's great botanical parks. The 750-metre allee of 134 Imperial Palms forms a colonnade that shadows every photograph of Rio's green interior. Beyond it: a Japanese Garden, Victoria amazonica lilies, and 6,500 Atlantic Forest species.

8 min → Rodrigo de Freitas Lagoon
2. Rodrigo de Freitas Lagoon
An 8.2km circuit of cycle path and promenade rings the lagoon, with kiosk restaurants at each cardinal point. The water hosted rowing and sprint canoeing at the 2016 Olympics. Pedal boats and canoes are available for rent; the views back to Cristo Redentor and the Dois Irmãos peaks are among the best in the city.

15 min → Instituto Moreira Salles
3. Instituto Moreira Salles
Brazil's foremost photography and cultural institute occupies a 1951 modernist residence designed by Olavo Redig de Campos, with a tropical garden by Roberto Burle Marx. The archive holds over 700,000 historical photographs and rotating exhibitions drawn from the collection of the Moreira Salles banking family.

Day 6
From Hotel: 10 min → Museu do Índio
1. Museu do Índio
Created by Darcy Ribeiro in 1953 and moved in 1978 to an 1880s mansion in Botafogo, this is Brazil's only national institution exclusively dedicated to indigenous peoples. Its 14,000 artifacts cover ceramics, textiles, ritual objects, and archives representing most of Brazil's present-day indigenous societies.

32 min → MAC Niterói
2. MAC Niterói
Oscar Niemeyer designed this museum at 84 — a 50-metre disc of white reinforced concrete hovering over Guanabara Bay on a single cylinder. The circular terrace takes in Rio's entire skyline across the water. The collection covers Brazilian contemporary art; the building is the real exhibit.

Local Tastes
Caipirinha
Brazil's national cocktail — cachaça, fresh lime, ice, and sugar. The quality gap between a well-made one and a bad one is enormous. Order it at Bar do Mineiro, any botequim, or on a sunset sailing tour.
Bar do Mineiro · Santa Teresa
Feijoada
A slow-cooked black bean stew with pork shoulder, ribs, and sausage — served on Saturdays throughout Rio with white rice, collard greens, farofa, and orange slices. The national dish, served seriously.
Bar do Mineiro · Santa Teresa
Pão de Queijo
Brazilian cheese bread made from tapioca starch — slightly chewy, hollow-crisp exterior, salty cheese centre, eaten hot in every café in the country. At its best at breakfast or late morning.
Confeitaria Colombo · Centro
Açaí Bowl
Thick frozen açaí puree topped with granola, banana, and honey — born as post-surf food on Rio's beaches and now consumed with competitive intensity citywide. Order from any beachfront kiosk on Copacabana.
Copacabana beach kiosks · Av. Atlântica
Churrasco
Brazilian barbecue is about one cut above all others: picanha — grilled whole and sliced at the table. The fat cap renders as it cooks. The rodízio format means it keeps arriving until you say stop.
Churrascaria Palace · Copacabana
Food Delivery
iFood
Foreign number: not accepted — a Brazilian number and CPF are both required; ask your hotel's front desk to place the order instead.
Brazil's dominant delivery platform with the widest selection in Rio, covering everything from neighbourhood lanchonetes to higher-end restaurants in Ipanema and Leblon. International visitors cannot register without a Brazilian CPF.
ifood.com.br
Rappi
Foreign number: not accepted — only a mobile number from one of the Latin American countries Rappi operates in works.
Covers Rio with groceries and restaurant delivery but requires a local Latin American number. Neither platform is practical for visitors without a Brazilian CPF; rely on the hotel concierge or room service instead.
rappi.com.br

Getting Around
Uber
Foreign number: accepted.
The most practical option for visitors across Rio's spread-out neighbourhoods. Reliable coverage from Santa Teresa and the Centro through Ipanema and Leblon; upfront pricing removes the haggling risk on tourist routes.
uber.com/br
99
Foreign number: not accepted — a Brazilian phone number is required to register.
Rio's other major ride app with competitive fares, but international visitors cannot register. Locals often use it alongside Uber to compare prices.
99app.com
CCR Barcas
Ferry from Praça XV to Niterói — every 10 min peak, every 30 min at night.
Rio de Janeiro has a ferry — operated by Barcas Rio. Route: Praça XV → Niterói.
barcasrio.com.br.

Heads Up
All Museums & Fort — Closed Monday
Museu do Amanhã, Parque das Ruínas, Forte de Copacabana, and MAC Niterói are closed Monday; schedule Days 1 and 3 for Tuesday through Sunday.
Corcovado — Book Tickets Before Arriving
The cog railway sells out on weekends; book at tremdocorcovado.rio at least 3–4 days ahead — early morning for clearest views.
MAC Niterói — Allow Extra Time for the Ferry
The ferry adds 20 minutes each way plus embarkation time; start Day 3 before 10:00am to allow enough time before closing.
Confeitaria Colombo — Closed Sunday
The café is closed Sunday; visit before noon on a weekday when the salon is quietest — it opens at 9:00am Monday through Friday.
Cristo Redentor — Morning for Best Visibility
Corcovado sits inside Atlantic Forest and is regularly enclosed by mist from mid-morning; clear views are most reliable before 11:00am.

Worth Knowing

Rio as Geology

The shape of this city is stranger than it looks. Rio was built in the spaces that granite would not let anything else be built — in the narrow valley floors between peaks that rise straight from the sea, on the thin coastal plain between mountains and Atlantic. Copacabana was not accessible from the rest of the city until a tunnel was blasted through the coastal rock at the end of the 19th century. The geography that makes this place so photogenic is exactly the geography that made it so difficult to build.

Selarón died on the stairs he spent over two decades tiling. He was found in January, on the steps he had declared his gift to the Brazilian people, surrounded by tile fragments collected from dozens of countries. The cause was never conclusively determined. He had told interviewers that he would only stop working on the staircase when he died. This turned out to be literally accurate.
